summary: ELSEWHERE is an interactive web tool that finds places on Earth that behave like any location on the Moon or Mars, and shows how to test there. Users pick a lunar or Martian surface cell, or jump straight to a mission site such as NASA's Artemis III candidate regions near the lunar south pole, Shackleton crater, Jezero or Gale. The tool compares 12,960 planetary cells, grouped into 42 environment types, with 333 Earth sites on six dimensions: terrain, thermal, illumination, water ice, surface material and dust. Each dimension stays separate instead of being collapsed into one score, so teams see where an analog is strong and where it falls short. For every Earth site, ELSEWHERE adds the months that reproduce conditions such as polar night or Mars-level sunlight, an engineering scale-transfer scenario that suggests how to adjust an Earth test, and links between lunar pits, Martian caves and Earth lava tubes. This helps mission teams choose, time and design analog field tests before going to the Moon or Mars.
details:
What it does

ELSEWHERE answers three questions that analog studies usually tackle one site at a time: where on Earth resembles a given place on the Moon or Mars, when in the year that Earth site behaves most alike, and how an Earth test should be adjusted to match the target. The journey has four stages: choose a world, choose a surface region (or a mission site), compare Earth analogs on a globe and a ranked list, then open a site report with satellite imagery, dimension-by-dimension similarity, monthly test windows, an engineering scenario and cave comparisons. Any report can be downloaded as a mission card with a link that reopens the same view.


Method: what is data-driven, and what is new

We do not train a black-box model to predict one "best" site. The pipeline chains global remote-sensing features, unsupervised prototype selection, distribution distances, multi-objective screening, information theory and dimensionless physics, and every step can be traced back to its data.

- Unsupervised coverage instead of a fixed number of targets. All 12,960 coarse Moon and Mars cells are kept. A farthest-first L-infinity cover in a robust-standardized fingerprint space adds representatives until every cell lies within a cover radius of 1.5 of one. The data, not a preset k, produced the 42 environment types (7 Moon, 35 Mars), and every cell keeps its link to its type.

- Terrain is not the only way in. Earth candidates come from a terrain shortlist plus a target-independent sample stratified by latitude and elevation, with NASA POWER environment data added. A site that looks different but matches on temperature, sunlight, water ice, material or dust can still qualify.

- Statistical similarity, kept per dimension. Wasserstein distance compares single-feature distributions, multivariate energy distance compares joint terrain fingerprints, and normalized proxy distances cover the environmental dimensions. The full distance vector is kept: there are no subjective weights, and missing values are never treated as zero.

- Multi-objective screening. A Pareto frontier, a minimax core that controls the worst dimension, and per-dimension champions, with a minimum spacing between sites, keep different kinds of similarity in one candidate pool instead of producing a single false "number one".

- Information-theoretic dimensionless learning. Following IT-π (Yuan & Lozano-Durán, 2025), mutual information picks the Buckingham Π representation that keeps the most information about a task output. Rover mobility uses real JPL Barefoot Rover telemetry (one 59-second run, 2,040 time-aligned samples), where the sinkage ratio carried the most information about wheel slip. The other five tasks use team-built physics-informed synthetic trials (800 per task) and are labelled as such.

- Physics-informed scale transfer. For each of the 3,347 Earth–planet pairs, a seeded bounded random search (7,000 trials in log space over four Earth-test controls) minimizes the largest log mismatch between the Earth and target Π groups. The output is a set of adjustment factors plus the remaining mismatch: a scenario from assumed inputs, not a measurement or a success rate.

- Evidence levels stay visible. Planetary remote sensing, Earth climatology, proxies, real telemetry and synthetic models are labelled separately, so users can see how strong each piece of evidence is.

Why it matters: most analog searches end with a ranked map. Ours continues to the experiment. It keeps several kinds of similarity without subjective weights, learns which dimensionless variables carry task information, and estimates how an Earth test should be adjusted to reproduce a Moon or Mars engineering regime: analog discovery plus experiment design.

What Earth cannot match

Every report names the weakest dimension of each pair, so gaps stay visible. For the Moon, the weakest dimension is thermal in 60% of the 558 Earth–Moon pairs and illumination in 30%: no Earth surface reaches lunar cold, and lunar lighting can only be approached in polar seasons, so those conditions need the right month or a thermal-vacuum chamber. For Mars, the gaps are spread across terrain (26% of 2,789 pairs), dust (22%), surface material (19%) and water ice (18%). Scale transfer narrows the engineering gap (median Π mismatch from 1.10 to 0.14 for the Moon and from 0.60 to 0.09 for Mars), but 26% of Moon pairs and 16% of Mars pairs keep a residual above 0.5, which the report shows as a limit the Earth test cannot close.

How it works

1. Global fingerprints. Terrain features (slope, roughness, relief, curvature, texture) come from NOAA ETOPO 2022 for Earth, LRO LOLA for the Moon and MGS MOLA for Mars. Mars albedo and thermal inertia come from MGS TES, and Earth climate from NASA POWER 2016–2025. Thermal, illumination, water-ice, surface-material and dust indicators are built on a common coarse grid and robust-standardized.

2. Planet environment types. A farthest-first coverage algorithm groups all 12,960 lunar and Martian cells into 42 representative types (7 Moon, 35 Mars) without discarding any cell.

3. Similarity per dimension. Earth–planet pairs are compared with Wasserstein and energy distances for distributions and normalized distances for environmental proxies. Each dimension is shown as a 0–1 similarity, the share of all study pairs that are less alike.

4. Shortlisting. A Pareto frontier, a minimax core and per-dimension champions keep different kinds of similarity: 3,347 Earth–planet pairs across 333 Earth sites.

5. Monthly test windows. NASA POWER monthly climatology and solar geometry flag the months that reproduce polar night, polar day, low sun angle, Mars-level cold, Mars-level or lunar-level sunlight and strong wind.

6. Engineering scale transfer. Each pair is assigned one of six engineering tests (rover mobility, drilling and sampling, thermal control, power continuity, ice resource operations, dust mitigation). Buckingham Π groups, with information-theoretic selection inspired by IT-π (Yuan & Lozano-Durán, 2025), are matched by bounded minimax optimization of four Earth-test controls. Rover mobility uses a real JPL Barefoot Rover run; the other five use team-built physics models.

7. Caves and pits. 61 lunar pits (LROC Pits Atlas) and Martian cave candidates are linked to 18 Earth caves and lava tubes by entrance size, depth and formation process.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission teams, students and researchers can screen the whole Moon and Mars instead of a few well-known sites, see each dimension's strengths and gaps, plan field campaigns in the right season, and start from a concrete recipe for adjusting Earth tests. Mission-site shortcuts tie the tool directly to the permanent lunar base question: for example, the Artemis III Haworth region leads to Sakha Republic in Siberia, closest on water ice, with December polar night as the best test window.

Tools and technologies

Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas-style CSV processing, Shapely) for data processing and modelling; a static website in HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with a custom WebGL globe and the Web Audio API; NASA GIBS and Solar System Treks imagery services; GitHub Pages for hosting.

Creativity

ELSEWHERE turns analog selection into an exploration experience: a planet-first journey, mission-site shortcuts, monthly test windows, engineering recipes, shareable mission cards and a layered soundtrack that changes with each stage.

Factors we considered

- No weighted total score: dimensions stay separate, and lists are ordered by the weakest chosen dimension.

- Missing data is never treated as zero or as similar.

- Modelled and proxy values are labelled as such.

- Engineering values are scenarios from assumed inputs, not site measurements or certified settings.

- Mission-site buttons use IAU feature centres and open the containing cell, not an exact landing point.

- Check against known analogs: of 20 widely used Moon and Mars analog sites (Atacama, Svalbard, Utah MDRS, Rio Tinto and others), 8 lie within 300 km of a site in our 333-site Earth pool. Those rank higher than random pool sites (mean normalized rank 0.30 vs 0.49, 41 pairs), but the difference is not significant (p = 0.15), comes mostly from Svalbard, and none reaches a top three. Classic analogs are often chosen for geology or logistics, which our six dimensions do not score; a finer Earth grid is the next step.

- The tool complements expert field selection and is not an official NASA site selection.

- Sound can be turned off with one switch, and the choice is remembered.
